title: A cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:6–8)

segments.voice: Yesterday, skolops, the thorn that stayed, and the grace that came with it. Your line was my grace is sufficient. Did you name your thorn? Day five hundred seventy-nine.

Paul spent years running a collection. Churches of Gentile believers, in Greece and Asia Minor, were asked to put money aside for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He mentions it in Romans and in both letters to Corinth. It was money, and it was also a sign: the newer churches sharing with the mother church that had given them the Gospel. In Second Corinthians he gives the subject a long stretch of the letter. He praises the churches of Macedonia, who gave out of deep poverty, beyond their means. Then he turns to Corinth, which had promised a lot and not yet delivered.
screen: `A COLLECTION FOR JERUSALEM.` → `MACEDONIA GAVE FROM POVERTY.` → `CORINTH HAD PROMISED.`

segments.voice: He starts with a farmer's rule: whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will reap generously. Then he says how to give: "Every one as he hath determined in his heart, not with sadness, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." Three things are packed in there. First, decide in your heart. Paul doesn't set an amount. Second, not with sadness: no grudging, no giving while silently resenting it. Third, not of necessity: not squeezed out by pressure or shame. The Greek word for cheerful is hilaros: glad, bright, ready. Paul seems to be echoing a line from the old Greek version of the book of Proverbs, which says God blesses a cheerful giver. Then he adds a promise: God is able to make all grace abound in you, so that you have enough, and enough left over for every good work. In Paul's picture, giving isn't a loss to be endured. It's seed, and God keeps you supplied with more. Catholics put this into practice in many ways. Almsgiving is one of the three traditional practices of Lent, with prayer and fasting. The Catechism counts giving to the poor among the works of mercy and calls it a work of justice pleasing to God. But Paul's interest here is less in the amount than in the face. Two people can put the same money in the basket. One with a sigh. One with a smile. Paul says God loves the second.
screen: `SOW SPARINGLY, REAP SPARINGLY.` · `DECIDED IN YOUR HEART.` · `NOT WITH SADNESS, NOT FORCED.` · `HILAROS: CHEERFUL.` · then, large: `GOD LOVETH A CHEERFUL GIVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a glad gift. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you could give today. Money to someone who needs it, your time, a meal, your full attention for ten minutes. Make it small enough that you can give it without a sigh. Now picture yourself giving it, and notice your face as you do. Is it tight, or easy? Decide it in your heart right now, so it isn't squeezed out of you later. If you pray, you can offer the gift to God before you give it. If you don't, simply decide, and let yourself be glad about it. The bell holds the time.
Hilaros. Greek for glad, bright, ready: the kind of giving God loves, decided in the heart, not squeezed out by sadness or pressure. Today's word.
Your line: cheerful. Today, give one thing with a smile, and make the smile real by keeping the gift small enough to enjoy. Day five hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics give through the parish collection at Mass, through Lenten almsgiving, and through charities such as the Society of St. Vincent de Paul; the Church counts almsgiving among the works of mercy.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line ushers say when the basket comes round.
what it means: give what you've decided in your heart, without grudging or pressure, because God loves a glad giver.
what a scholar hears: hilaros, an echo of Greek Proverbs 22:8, inside Paul's years-long collection for Jerusalem's poor.

sources.quoted: Every one as he hath determined in his heart, not with sadness, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.

notes: The collection appears in 1 Corinthians 16, 2 Corinthians 8–9 and Romans 15 ('three different letters'). Confirm.
Septuagint Proverbs 22:8a ('God blesses a cheerful man and a giver'): echo stated as 'seems to'. Confirm.
hilaros → Latin hilaris → English 'hilarious': standard etymology. Confirm.
CCC 2447 on almsgiving as a work of justice pleasing to God; CCC 1434 on prayer, fasting, almsgiving. Confirm.
